sections.overview: The Darwin termite is a distinctive large-bodied member of the family Mastotermitidae, native to tropical northern Australia.
sections.identification: It is a large termite; unlike many termites, it has no true worker caste.
sections.habitat: It occurs in tropical northern Australia, where colonies live in galleries and nests associated with trees, logs and other wood.
sections.diet: It consumes wood and other plant material and can damage living trees, timber and crops near settlements and plantations.
sections.behavior: It lives in social colonies; colony size is generally small in natural settings but can grow in built-up areas.
sections.reproduction: Termite colonies generally produce winged reproductive forms that disperse and found new colonies; species-specific breeding data are scarce.
sections.ecology: It helps decompose wood and plant matter, but is also an economically important timber pest in northern Australia.
sections.conservation: It is documented as a damaging timber and crop pest in tropical northern Australia; the references give no population-trend estimate.
